specStatements.text: Newton’s First Law:
If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and:
• the object is stationary, the object remains stationary
• the object is moving, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction. So the object continues to move at the same velocity.
So, when a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force.
So, the velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object.
Students should be able to apply Newton’s First Law to explain the motion of objects moving with a uniform velocity and objects where the speed and/or direction changes.
(HT only) The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia.
Newton’s Second Law:
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
As an equation:
resultant force = mass × acceleration
F = m a
force, F, in newtons, N
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
(HT only) Students should be able to explain that:
• inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object
• inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration.
Students should be able to estimate the speed, accelerations and forces involved in large accelerations for everyday road transport.
Students should recognise and be able to use the symbol that indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, ̴

Required practical activity 7: investigate the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass, and the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 2 and 3.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Newton’s Third Law:
Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
Students should be able to apply Newton’s Third Law to examples of equilibrium situations.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 2 and 3.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Required practical activity 7 is treated here as a laboratory skills requirement, and the skills exercised are held to the three apparatus-and-techniques statements the specification names for it: making and recording measurements accurately (the mass of the trolley and of the hanging masses, the distance between light gates, times), measuring and observing the effects of forces (the pull of the hanging weight on the trolley), and measuring motion, including the determination of speed and rate of change of speed. No apparatus or technique from outside those three is introduced under this practical, and the numbered AT descriptors themselves are never set as recall - they describe what a student does at the bench, not content to be learned and examined.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The working scientifically and mathematical skills are developed through the practical itself - choosing the independent, dependent and control variables, recognising why the total accelerating mass must be held constant, plotting acceleration against resultant force and against mass, drawing a line of best fit and reading a gradient - rather than being taught as a separate body of knowledge. Nothing in this material examines the WS or MS statements as content in their own right, and no skill is assessed here that the practical does not naturally require.

concepts.definition: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object's velocity does not change: a stationary object remains stationary, and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed and in the same direction. It follows that the velocity of an object - its speed and/or its direction - will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. The law says nothing about there being no forces; it is about the resultant of the forces being zero.

concepts.term: Zero resultant force on a stationary object
concepts.definition: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and the object is stationary, the object remains stationary. A book on a table has its weight pulling it down and the table pushing it up; these forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant is zero and the book stays where it is. Forces are certainly acting - what is zero is their resultant.

concepts.term: Zero resultant force on a moving object
concepts.definition: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and the object is moving, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction. So the object continues to move at the same velocity. No forward force is needed to keep an object moving; a force is only needed to change how it moves. On a frictionless surface an object given a push would carry on at that speed for ever.

When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force. The engine's driving force is not larger than friction and air resistance - if it were, the resultant force would not be zero and the vehicle would be accelerating. The driving force is needed only to cancel the resistive forces, which is why a vehicle slows down as soon as the driving force is removed.

The velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. Because velocity includes direction, an object travelling round a bend at a constant speed has a changing velocity, so there must be a resultant force on it. A change of speed, a change of direction, or both, each require a resultant force.

To explain a motion, first decide whether the velocity is constant. If the object is stationary or moving with a uniform velocity, the forces on it must have a resultant of zero, so the opposing forces are equal in size - a skydiver at terminal velocity, a car at steady speed, a crate at rest. If the speed and/or the direction is changing, there must be a resultant force, and it acts in the direction of the change: forwards for a car speeding up, backwards for a train braking, towards the centre for a vehicle turning a corner.

The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. Inertia is a tendency, not a force: nothing pushes a moving object along, it simply keeps moving because no resultant force is changing its velocity. Inertia is why a passenger continues to move forwards when a bus brakes sharply.

The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Doubling the resultant force on a given object doubles its acceleration; doubling the mass while keeping the resultant force the same halves the acceleration. The acceleration is always in the same direction as the resultant force.

Newton's Second Law as an equation is resultant force = mass x acceleration, written F = m a. This is one of the equations that must be recalled and applied. The force in the equation is always the resultant force, not one of the individual forces: for a car with a driving force of 4800 N and resistive forces of 1800 N, the F to use is 3000 N.

concepts.term: Quantities and units in F = m a
concepts.definition: In F = m a the quantities are: force, F, in newtons, N; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s². Masses given in grams must be converted to kilograms before use, and a mass must never be entered as a weight in newtons. Acceleration is in m/s², not m/s - m/s is a speed.

The equation can be rearranged to find whichever quantity is unknown: a = F / m to find an acceleration, and m = F / a to find a mass. Both rearrangements involve dividing, never multiplying. A resultant force of 60 N on a mass of 15 kg gives a = 60 / 15 = 4.0 m/s²; a resultant force of 60 N producing an acceleration of 4.0 m/s² implies a mass of 60 / 4.0 = 15 kg.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. If two objects are acted on by the same resultant force, the one that changes velocity less readily - the one with the smaller acceleration - has the greater inertial mass. It is measured in kilograms, like any other mass.

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. In symbols this is m = F / a, which is simply Newton's Second Law rearranged. Because it is a force divided by an acceleration, its unit is N divided by m/s², which is the kilogram - so inertial mass is a mass, not a force.

concepts.term: Estimating speeds, accelerations and forces on the road
concepts.definition: Sensible everyday figures let you estimate the forces involved in large accelerations for road transport. A typical urban speed is about 13 m/s (30 mph) and a motorway speed about 31 m/s (70 mph); a family car has a mass of the order of 1000 to 1500 kg. A car accelerating briskly from rest to 27 m/s in about 9 s has an acceleration of roughly 3 m/s², and emergency braking can reach around 10 m/s². Putting these into F = m a gives resultant forces of the order of several thousand newtons - thousands, not tens.

The symbol ~ placed before a value shows that the value is approximate: it is an estimate rather than an exact answer. Writing 'resultant force ~ 4000 N' means the force is about 4000 N, a figure obtained from rounded, typical values. An estimate should still be worked out properly from an equation and quoted to one or two significant figures; the symbol signals the precision of the answer, not carelessness in getting it.

A trolley on a runway is pulled by a string that passes over a pulley at the end of the bench to a hanging mass holder; the weight of the hanging masses provides the accelerating force. The acceleration is found from light gates and a data logger, or from a tape produced by a ticker timer. To vary the force while keeping the mass of the object constant, masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger rather than simply added to the hanger, so that the total mass being accelerated stays the same. Friction is compensated for by tilting the runway slightly until the trolley runs at a steady speed after a gentle push.

In the second investigation the hanging masses are left unchanged, so the accelerating force is constant, and extra masses are loaded onto the trolley to increase the mass of the object. The acceleration is measured again for each mass. The independent variable is the mass, the dependent variable is the acceleration, and the control variable is the force.

With the mass constant, a graph of acceleration against resultant force is a straight line through the origin, showing that acceleration is proportional to the resultant force. With the force constant, acceleration falls as mass rises and a graph of acceleration against mass is a curve, not a straight line; plotting acceleration against 1 / mass straightens it, showing that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Together the two results are Newton's Second Law.

Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite. The two forces are always the same size, however different the two objects are: in a collision between a car and a lorry, the car pushes on the lorry exactly as hard as the lorry pushes on the car. Neither force comes first - they exist together for as long as the interaction lasts.

concepts.term: Identifying a Newton's Third Law pair
concepts.definition: The two forces of a third law pair are equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type (both contact forces, or both gravitational, for example), and - crucially - they act on two different objects. Because they act on different objects they can never cancel each other out; only forces acting on the same object can be added to give a resultant.

concepts.term: Newton's Third Law in equilibrium situations
concepts.definition: For a person standing still on the floor, the floor pushes up on the person and the person pushes down on the floor: equal, opposite, and acting on different objects, so this is a third law pair. The person's weight and the floor's upward push are a different matter - both act on the person, and they happen to be equal because the person is in equilibrium under Newton's First Law. In equilibrium the resultant force on each object is zero, and every interaction contributes a pair of equal and opposite forces.

concepts.term: Newton's First Law and Third Law compared
concepts.definition: Balanced forces (First Law) and a third law pair (Third Law) are different ideas that are easily confused. Balanced forces act on the same single object, may be of different types, and are equal only because that object's velocity is not changing. A third law pair acts on two different objects, is always of the same type, and is always equal whether or not anything is in equilibrium.

misconceptions.question: A puck slides across smooth ice at a steady speed. Is a forward force acting on it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its velocity is not changing, so the resultant force on it is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: Something must be pushing it forwards, otherwise it would stop - a moving object needs a force to keep it moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every moving object in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that experience and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause.
misconceptions.correction: A force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity for ever with no forward force at all.

misconceptions.question: A crate sits still on the floor. Are there forces on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - its weight acts downwards and the floor pushes up on it. The two are equal, so the resultant force is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: If it is not moving, no forces can be acting on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Forces are introduced as pushes and pulls that make things happen, so a situation where nothing happens looks like a situation with no forces. Weight and the contact force from a surface are also invisible.
misconceptions.correction: Newton's First Law is about the resultant force being zero, not about there being no forces. Draw every force on the object first, then decide what their resultant is.

misconceptions.question: The forces on a moving trolley are balanced. What happens to it?
misconceptions.correct: It continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so at the same velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: Balanced forces bring a moving object to a stop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet balanced forces first in examples of stationary objects, so 'balanced' becomes attached to 'at rest'. Real trolleys also do stop, because the forces on them are not in fact balanced.
misconceptions.correction: Zero resultant force means no change of velocity. If the trolley was moving at 2 m/s it goes on at 2 m/s; only a resultant force could slow it down.

misconceptions.question: A lorry travels along a motorway at a constant 25 m/s. How does the driving force compare with the resistive forces?
misconceptions.correct: They are equal - when a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force.
misconceptions.misconception: The driving force must be bigger, or the lorry could not keep going forwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The engine is obviously doing something, and students expect the direction of travel to belong to the larger force. Fuel is being used, so it feels as though the forward force must be winning.
misconceptions.correction: A larger driving force would give a resultant force forwards, and the lorry would be speeding up. Constant speed in a straight line means zero resultant force, so the forces are exactly equal.

misconceptions.question: A car drives round a roundabout at a constant 8 m/s. Is there a resultant force on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Its direction is changing, so its velocity is changing, so a resultant force must be acting.
misconceptions.misconception: The speed is constant, so nothing is changing and the resultant force is zero.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use 'speed' and 'velocity' as synonyms in everyday talk, so a constant speedometer reading looks like unchanging motion.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is speed and/or direction. Change either one and the velocity has changed, which requires a resultant force - here one directed towards the centre of the roundabout.

misconceptions.question: What is inertia?
misconceptions.correct: It is the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.
misconceptions.misconception: Inertia is a force that keeps a moving object going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word is used in everyday speech as though it were a push, and it is introduced alongside forces. Students still looking for a cause of continued motion seize on it as that cause.
misconceptions.correction: Inertia is a property, not a force. It never appears on a free body diagram and it is never measured in newtons. Continued motion needs no cause; only a change of motion does.

misconceptions.question: The same resultant force acts on a heavy trolley and a light trolley. Which accelerates more?
misconceptions.correct: The light one. Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavy one, because heavy things have more force behind them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the resultant force with the object's weight, and know that heavy objects fall hard and hit hard, so they associate mass with a bigger effect rather than with resistance to change.
misconceptions.correction: The resultant force is stated to be the same for both. In a = F / m, increasing m with F fixed makes a smaller, so the heavier trolley accelerates less.

misconceptions.question: The mass of an object is doubled while the resultant force on it is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: It halves - acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
misconceptions.misconception: It doubles, because acceleration and mass are proportional.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Proportional' is remembered from the first half of the sentence and applied to both quantities. In F = m a the mass and the acceleration sit side by side, which looks like a direct relationship.
misconceptions.correction: Read the law in two halves: acceleration is proportional to resultant force, and inversely proportional to mass. Rearranged, a = F / m - mass is on the bottom, so more mass means less acceleration.

misconceptions.question: A car has a driving force of 4800 N and resistive forces of 1800 N. Which force goes into F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: The resultant force, 4800 - 1800 = 3000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: The driving force, 4800 N, because that is the force making the car accelerate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The driving force is the one that looks responsible for the motion, and questions often name it first. The word 'resultant' is easily skipped when reading the equation.
misconceptions.correction: F in the equation is always the resultant of all the forces acting. Work out the resultant first, then substitute; using 4800 N here would overstate the acceleration by 60 per cent.

misconceptions.question: An object weighs 12 N on Earth. What value of m goes into F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: Not 12. The mass must be in kilograms; a weight in newtons is a force, not a mass.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass is 12, since that is the number given for how heavy it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'weight' and 'mass' mean the same thing, and both are quoted as single numbers describing how heavy something is.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change; weight is a force in newtons. Only a mass in kg may be substituted for m, and grams must be converted first.

misconceptions.question: A car reaches 27 m/s from rest in 9 s. What value of a goes into F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: 3 m/s² - the change in velocity divided by the time taken.
misconceptions.misconception: 27, because that is how fast it is going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The speed is the number the question gives most prominently, and students who have not separated speed from acceleration take the largest available figure for 'how fast it speeds up'.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity, so it must be found by dividing a change of velocity by a time. Substituting the speed instead of the acceleration inflates the force roughly ninefold here.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of acceleration in F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: Metres per second squared, m/s².
misconceptions.misconception: Metres per second, m/s, like all the other motion quantities.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed and velocity are met first and both use m/s, so m/s becomes the default unit for anything to do with motion; the squared sign looks like a decoration.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration tells you how many metres per second the velocity changes in each second, so its unit is (m/s) per s, written m/s². Only that unit gives newtons when multiplied by kilograms.

misconceptions.question: Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. What unit does it have?
misconceptions.correct: The kilogram - N divided by m/s² is kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Newtons, because the definition starts with a force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'force' appears in the definition, and students expect the unit of a defined quantity to be the unit of the first quantity named in it.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing changes the unit. Inertial mass is a mass and is measured in kilograms; if it came out in newtons it could not be substituted for m in F = m a.

misconceptions.question: Is the inertial mass of a trolley the same as the mass you would measure on a balance?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Inertial mass is that same mass, described by how hard it is to change the object's velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: Inertial mass is a separate quantity that an object only has when it is being accelerated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'inertial' makes it sound like a new quantity, and it is introduced through an experiment about acceleration, so it seems to belong only to moving objects.
misconceptions.correction: Inertial mass is a way of defining mass, not a second kind of mass. A 2 kg trolley has an inertial mass of 2 kg whether it is at rest or accelerating.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical 7, why are masses moved from the trolley to the hanger rather than just added to the hanger?
misconceptions.correct: Because the total mass being accelerated - trolley plus hanging masses - must be kept constant while only the force is changed.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass that matters is the trolley's, so adding masses to the hanger changes only the force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The trolley is the object students are watching, and the hanging masses look like part of the apparatus that supplies the force rather than part of the moving system.
misconceptions.correction: The string makes the trolley and the hanging masses accelerate together as one system, so their combined mass is the m in F = m a. Transferring masses raises the force while holding that total fixed.

misconceptions.question: Why is the runway tilted slightly before the readings are taken?
misconceptions.correct: To compensate for friction, so that the pull of the hanging weight is the resultant force on the trolley.
misconceptions.misconception: Friction on a smooth runway is far too small to matter, so the tilt is not really needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The trolley runs freely and the friction is not visible, and textbook questions routinely say 'ignore friction'. The tilt then looks like an odd extra step.
misconceptions.correction: Uncompensated friction means part of the pull is used up opposing it, so the measured acceleration is too small and the graph of acceleration against force cuts the force axis instead of passing through the origin.

misconceptions.question: With the force kept constant, what shape is a graph of acceleration against mass?
misconceptions.correct: A curve falling away towards the mass axis, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
misconceptions.misconception: A straight line sloping downwards, since the acceleration goes down steadily as mass goes up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat any relationship where one quantity falls as the other rises as linear, and a straight line is the easiest line of best fit to draw.
misconceptions.correction: Doubling the mass halves the acceleration rather than reducing it by a fixed amount, which gives a curve. Plot acceleration against 1 / mass and the points fall on a straight line through the origin.

misconceptions.question: When you push on a wall, which comes first - your push or the wall's push back?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. The two forces exist together for as long as you and the wall interact.
misconceptions.misconception: You act first and then the wall reacts, a moment later.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The old wording 'action and reaction' suggests a sequence, and in everyday language a reaction is a response to something that has already happened.
misconceptions.correction: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite - simultaneously. There is no delay and no way to say which force caused the other.

misconceptions.question: If the forces in a Newton's Third Law pair are equal and opposite, why does anything ever accelerate?
misconceptions.correct: Because the two forces act on two different objects, so they never appear in the same resultant.
misconceptions.misconception: They must cancel out, so no object could ever have a resultant force on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn to cancel equal and opposite forces when finding a resultant, and apply that habit without checking which object each force acts on.
misconceptions.correction: Only forces acting on the same object can be combined into a resultant. A horse pulls the cart and the cart pulls the horse; the cart's motion depends only on the forces acting on the cart.

misconceptions.question: A book rests on a table. Are the book's weight and the table's upward push a Newton's Third Law pair?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both act on the book, so they are balanced forces under the First Law, not a Third Law pair.
misconceptions.misconception: They are equal and opposite, so they must be the action and reaction pair.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two forces are the ones drawn on the diagram, and they really are equal and opposite here, so the definition seems to fit.
misconceptions.correction: A Third Law pair acts on two different objects and is always the same type of force. The partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table; the partner of the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth.

misconceptions.question: A car collides with a much heavier lorry. Which vehicle exerts the larger force?
misconceptions.correct: Neither - the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
misconceptions.misconception: The lorry, because it is bigger and heavier, so it hits harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The damage is far worse on the car, and students read the outcome back into the forces. Everyday language about a heavy vehicle 'hitting harder' reinforces it.
misconceptions.correction: The forces are equal; the accelerations are not. The same size force produces a much larger acceleration on the smaller mass, which is why the car is damaged more.

misconceptions.question: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 4000 N'. What does the symbol mean?
misconceptions.correct: It indicates an approximate value or approximate answer - about 4000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: It means the number is only a guess, so the working and the size of the answer do not really matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Approximate' sounds like permission to be vague, and estimates are set without exact data, so students think no method is expected.
misconceptions.correction: An estimate is calculated from an equation using rounded but sensible values, and is then quoted to one or two significant figures with the symbol in front. A wildly wrong order of magnitude is still wrong.

misconceptions.question: Roughly what resultant force accelerates a family car briskly away from traffic lights?
misconceptions.correct: Of the order of a few thousand newtons - around 4000 N for a 1200 kg car at about 3 m/s².
misconceptions.misconception: A few hundred newtons, because that already sounds like a big push.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only forces students have handled are weights of laboratory masses, a few newtons at most, so a few hundred newtons feels enormous by comparison.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply through: a car's mass is around a thousand kilograms, so even a modest acceleration of 3 m/s² needs thousands of newtons. Always finish the estimate with F = m a rather than judging by feel.

misconceptions.question: A resultant force of 60 N gives an object an acceleration of 4.0 m/s². How do you find the mass?
misconceptions.correct: Divide: m = F / a = 60 / 4.0 = 15 kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the two numbers given, 60 x 4.0 = 240 kg.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember F = m a as 'the numbers multiply' and, unsure how to rearrange, multiply whatever they are given rather than dividing.
misconceptions.correction: Cover the quantity you want in the formula triangle, or divide both sides by a. Check the answer by substituting back: 15 x 4.0 = 60 N, which matches, while 240 x 4.0 = 960 N does not.

misconceptions.question: A car has a driving force of 4800 N forwards and resistive forces of 1800 N backwards. What is the resultant force?
misconceptions.correct: 3000 N forwards - the forces are in opposite directions, so they subtract.
misconceptions.misconception: 6600 N, because you add the two forces together to get the total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Resultant' is heard as 'total', and adding is the operation students default to when two numbers are given for the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Direction decides the operation. Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract, and the resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

misconceptions.question: Is any pair of equal and opposite forces a Newton's Third Law pair?
misconceptions.correct: No. The two forces must act on two different objects, and be the same type of force.
misconceptions.misconception: If two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, that is what makes them a Third Law pair.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The law is usually remembered as the phrase 'equal and opposite', and the rest of the definition - two objects, one interaction - is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which object each force acts on. Two forces on the same object are balanced forces under the First Law; a Third Law pair always comes from one interaction between two objects.

mcqs.stem: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes up on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?

options.text: No forces act on it at all, and that is why it stays still.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think 'nothing is happening' must mean 'no forces', even though the question names two of them.

options.text: The resultant force on it is zero, so it stays stationary.
options.rationale: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and a stationary object remains stationary.

options.text: Its weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.
options.rationale: The two forces are equal and opposite, so students label them action and reaction; both act on the crate, so they are balanced forces, not a pair.

options.text: The two forces add to give 800 N pressing downwards.
options.rationale: Picked by students who add force magnitudes without regard to direction.

mcqs.stem: A puck slides across a level ice rink in a straight line at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?

options.text: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
options.rationale: The most common error in mechanics: treating motion itself, rather than change of motion, as needing a force.

options.text: It acts backwards, so the puck is gradually slowing down.
options.rationale: Students who expect every real object to slow down ignore the statement that friction can be ignored.

options.text: It is 4 N forwards, since the steady speed is 4 m/s.
options.rationale: Reads the speed as if it were the force, a substitution error made when no other number is available.

options.text: It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
options.rationale: The speed and the direction are both constant, so the velocity is constant, which by Newton's First Law means the resultant force is zero.

mcqs.stem: A lorry travels along a straight, level motorway at a constant 25 m/s. What is true of the horizontal forces on it?

options.text: The driving force is larger than the resistive forces.
options.rationale: Students expect the direction of travel to belong to the bigger force, and the engine is clearly working.

options.text: The resistive forces are larger than the driving force.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who know friction and air resistance are always present and assume they must dominate.

options.text: Only a driving force acts, as nothing is slowing it.
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe a forward force alone is what keeps a vehicle moving.

options.text: The driving force and the resistive forces are equal.
options.rationale: When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force, so the resultant force is zero.

mcqs.stem: A car is driven round a roundabout at a constant speed of 8 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?

options.text: Yes, because its direction, and so its velocity, is changing.
options.rationale: Velocity is speed and/or direction, so a change of direction is a change of velocity and requires a resultant force.

options.text: No, because its speed stays the same all the way round.
options.rationale: Treats speed and velocity as the same quantity, so a steady speedometer reading looks like unchanging motion.

options.text: No, but a forward force is needed to keep the car moving.
options.rationale: Combines the belief that motion needs a force with the belief that steady speed means equilibrium.

options.text: Yes, but only at the moment the wheel is first turned.
options.rationale: Appeals to students who link the force to the driver's action rather than to the continuing change of direction.

mcqs.stem: A skydiver falls at a steady terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains this using Newton's First Law?

options.text: Air resistance is now larger than her weight, so she is gradually pushed back upwards.
options.rationale: Students who know air resistance grows with speed assume it must overtake the weight rather than only match it.

options.text: Her weight is still larger than air resistance, and that is what keeps her moving down.
options.rationale: Motion downwards is credited to a net downward force, the classic 'motion needs a force' error.

options.text: Air resistance now equals her weight, so the resultant force is zero and her velocity is constant.
options.rationale: Zero resultant force means a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction - a constant velocity.

options.text: No forces act on her at all now, which is why her velocity has stopped changing.
options.rationale: Equates 'balanced' with 'absent', so a constant velocity is read as an absence of forces.

mcqs.stem: A train is braking as it comes into a station. Which statement about the forces on the train is correct?

options.text: The forward force is smaller now but still larger than the braking force.
options.rationale: Students who think forward motion requires a net forward force cannot allow the resultant to point backwards.

options.text: The resultant force acts backwards, opposite to the direction of travel.
options.rationale: The velocity is decreasing, so there must be a resultant force, and it acts in the direction of the change - backwards.

options.text: The forces are now balanced, and balanced forces are what bring it to rest.
options.rationale: Attaches 'balanced' to 'stopping' rather than to 'no change of velocity'.

options.text: The resultant force acts forwards but is smaller than it was before.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who accept a change of force but keep it pointing the way the train is travelling.

mcqs.stem: The tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or of uniform motion has a name. Which statement gives it correctly?

options.text: Inertia, which is the force that keeps a moving object going forwards.
options.rationale: Right word, wrong category: students who still want a cause for continued motion make inertia into that cause.

options.text: Momentum, which is a property an object has only while it is moving.
options.rationale: A plausible near-miss, since momentum is also associated with keeping going, but it does not apply to an object at rest.

options.text: Inertia, which is the tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification calls inertia, and it names it as a tendency rather than as a force.

options.text: Weight, since a heavy object is harder to get moving than a light one.
options.rationale: Uses weight where mass is meant, and confuses the property with the gravitational force on the object.

mcqs.stem: Which statement of Newton's Second Law is correct?

options.text: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and proportional to mass.
options.rationale: 'Proportional' from the first half of the law is carried over to the second half, where it should be inversely.

options.text: Acceleration is proportional to mass and inversely proportional to force.
options.rationale: Swaps the roles of force and mass, an error made by students who associate large mass with a large effect.

options.text: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass.
options.rationale: This is the law as the specification states it: doubling the resultant force doubles the acceleration, doubling the mass halves it.

options.text: Force is proportional to acceleration and inversely proportional to mass.
options.rationale: Attractive because the first clause is true, but F = m a makes force proportional to mass, not inversely proportional to it.

mcqs.stem: Which equation is Newton's Second Law as the specification states it?

options.text: acceleration = mass x resultant force
options.rationale: Written by students who believe a larger mass gives a larger acceleration for the same force.

options.text: mass = resultant force x acceleration
options.rationale: The rearrangement error of multiplying the two given quantities instead of dividing.

options.text: resultant force = mass / acceleration
options.rationale: Keeps force as the subject but divides, chosen by students who half-remember a formula triangle.

options.text: resultant force = mass x acceleration
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification gives it, F = m a, and it must be recalled.

mcqs.stem: Which set of units is correct for the quantities in F = m a?

options.text: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s
options.rationale: Uses the speed unit for acceleration, because m/s is the unit met first for motion.

options.text: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s²
options.rationale: Force in newtons, mass in kilograms and acceleration in metres per second squared, exactly as the specification lists them.

options.text: F in N, m in N, a in m/s²
options.rationale: Treats mass as a weight in newtons, the standard mass and weight confusion.

options.text: F in N, m in g, a in m/s²
options.rationale: Leaves the mass in grams; a mass must be converted to kilograms before it is substituted.

mcqs.stem: A trolley of mass 0.80 kg has a resultant force of 2.0 N acting on it. What is its acceleration?

options.text: 1.6 m/s²
options.rationale: Multiplies the force by the mass instead of dividing, the usual response to an unfamiliar rearrangement.
Divides the mass by the force, putting the quantities the wrong way round in a = F / m.

options.text: 2.8 m/s²
options.rationale: Adds the two numbers, a fallback when the relationship is not recalled at all.

options.text: 2.5 m/s²

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 4800 N and resistive forces of 1800 N acting on it. What is its acceleration?

options.text: 4.0 m/s²
options.rationale: Uses the driving force alone as F, ignoring the resistive forces when finding the resultant.

options.text: 5.5 m/s²
options.rationale: Adds the two forces to get 6600 N, treating 'resultant' as 'total' regardless of direction.

options.text: 2.5 m/s²
options.rationale: The resultant force is 4800 - 1800 = 3000 N, so a = 3000 / 1200 = 2.5 m/s².

options.text: 1.5 m/s²
options.rationale: Uses the resistive force alone, picked by students who take the last force mentioned.

mcqs.stem: A resultant force of 60 N gives an object an acceleration of 4.0 m/s². What is the mass of the object?

options.text: 15 kg
options.rationale: m = F / a = 60 / 4.0 = 15 kg, which checks out because 15 x 4.0 = 60 N.

options.text: 240 kg
options.rationale: Multiplies the two given values instead of dividing them.
Divides the wrong way round, giving a mass far too small to be checked by substitution.

options.text: 56 kg
options.rationale: Subtracts the acceleration from the force, a last resort when no relationship is recalled.

mcqs.stem: The resultant force on an object is doubled, and at the same time its mass is doubled. What happens to its acceleration?

options.text: It stays the same, as the two changes cancel each other out.
options.rationale: a = F / m, and doubling both the numerator and the denominator leaves the quotient unchanged.

options.text: It is four times as large, as both changes increase it.
options.rationale: Takes acceleration to be proportional to both quantities, so the two doublings multiply together.

options.text: It is halved, because the greater mass has the bigger effect.
options.rationale: Assumes mass outweighs force, so the object must end up harder to accelerate.

options.text: It is doubled, because the resultant force has been doubled.
options.rationale: Applies only the first half of the law and overlooks the change of mass.

mcqs.stem: Two trolleys are pushed with the same resultant force. Trolley A proves much harder to speed up than trolley B. What does this show?

options.text: Trolley A has a larger inertia force acting on it.
options.rationale: Turns inertia into a force resisting the push, rather than a property of the object.

options.text: Trolley A weighs more, and weight is what resists.
options.rationale: Substitutes weight for mass, so the resistance to acceleration is credited to the wrong quantity.

options.text: Both have equal inertial mass; A just has more mass.
options.rationale: Treats inertial mass as a separate quantity from the mass measured on a balance.

options.text: Trolley A has the greater inertial mass of the two.
options.rationale: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, so the harder trolley has more of it.

mcqs.stem: How is inertial mass defined, and what unit does it have?

options.text: The ratio of acceleration over force, measured in kg.
options.rationale: Inverts the ratio; tempting because a = F / m is the rearrangement students use most often.

options.text: The force needed to hold an object still, measured in N.
options.rationale: Makes inertial mass a force because the word force appears in its definition.

options.text: The ratio of force over acceleration, measured in kg.
options.rationale: Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration, and N divided by m/s² is the kilogram.

options.text: The force with which an object resists a push, in N.
options.rationale: Combines the idea of inertia as a force with the unit that would follow from it.

mcqs.stem: A family car of mass about 1200 kg accelerates hard, reaching 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s. Estimate the resultant force on the car.

options.rationale: Substitutes the speed of 27 m/s for the acceleration, inflating the force roughly ninefold.
Chosen by students whose sense of scale for forces comes from laboratory masses.
The acceleration is 27 / 9 = 3 m/s², so F = 1200 x 3 = 3600 N, about 4000 N.
Divides the mass by the time, a combination of the given numbers that leaves the units meaningless.

mcqs.stem: A car pulls away from traffic lights and reaches 13 m/s in about 6 s. Which is the best estimate of its acceleration?

options.text: ~ 2 m/s²
options.rationale: 13 / 6 is about 2, a realistic acceleration for ordinary road transport.

options.text: ~ 78 m/s²
options.rationale: Multiplies the two given values whenever the rearrangement is uncertain.

options.text: ~ 13 m/s²
options.rationale: Reads the speed reached as the acceleration, ignoring the time taken to reach it.
Divides the time by the speed, giving the reciprocal of the correct answer.

mcqs.stem: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 4000 N' at the end of a calculation. What does the symbol tell the reader?

options.text: That the value is a guess, so precision was not needed.
options.rationale: Reads 'approximate' as permission to abandon method and check on the size of the answer.

options.text: That the value is approximate rather than exact.
options.rationale: The symbol indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, obtained from rounded but sensible figures.

options.text: That the value was not worked out from an equation.
options.rationale: Assumes an estimate is judged by eye; estimates are still calculated, using rounded data.

options.text: That the force was measured to within about 4000 N.
options.rationale: Confuses the approximation symbol with a statement of measurement uncertainty.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 7, a student investigates how the resultant force affects the acceleration of a trolley. What must be kept constant?

options.text: Only the mass of the trolley, not the hanging masses.
options.rationale: Treats the hanging masses as part of the apparatus supplying the force rather than part of the moving system.

options.text: The total mass accelerated, trolley and hanging masses.
options.rationale: The trolley and the hanging masses accelerate together as one system, so masses are transferred between them to change the force without changing the total mass.

options.text: The friction, which is small enough to ignore here.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume a smooth runway makes friction irrelevant rather than something to compensate.

options.text: The number of masses on the holder for each run.
options.rationale: Names the quantity that is deliberately varied, an easy slip when control and independent variables are confused.

mcqs.stem: In the second part of Required practical activity 7 the accelerating force is kept constant while masses are added to the trolley. What happens, and what shape is a graph of acceleration against mass?

options.text: Acceleration falls, and the graph is a straight line sloping down.
options.rationale: Right trend, wrong shape: any falling relationship is assumed to be linear.

options.text: Acceleration rises, and the graph is a straight line sloping up.
options.rationale: Held by students who think acceleration is proportional to mass rather than inversely proportional.

options.text: Acceleration stays the same, so the graph is a horizontal line.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a constant force must always give a constant acceleration.

options.text: Acceleration falls, and the graph is a curve, not a straight line.
options.rationale: Doubling the mass halves the acceleration, so the curve falls away towards the mass axis; a plot against 1 / mass would be straight.

mcqs.stem: A student plots acceleration against resultant force for a trolley of constant mass. The line of best fit is straight but crosses the force axis at 0.4 N instead of passing through the origin. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Friction can be ignored, so the intercept must be a plotting slip.
options.rationale: Students who believe friction is negligible must explain the intercept away as an error.

options.text: Friction on the runway was not properly compensated for.
options.rationale: Part of the pull is used opposing friction, so no acceleration is produced until the pull exceeds it - which shifts the intercept along the force axis.

options.text: The hanging masses were not counted in the mass accelerated.
options.rationale: A real error, but one that changes the gradient of the line rather than producing an intercept.

options.text: The two light gates were set too close together on the runway.
options.rationale: Gate separation affects the precision of each reading, not where a straight line meets the axis.

mcqs.stem: Two objects interact. What does Newton's Third Law say about the forces they exert on each other?

options.text: The first object acts and the second one reacts just after.
options.rationale: The wording 'action and reaction' suggests a sequence, and in everyday speech a reaction follows an action.

options.text: The larger object exerts the larger of the two forces.
options.rationale: Reads the greater damage done by a heavy object back into the size of the force it exerts.

options.text: They are equal in size and act in the same direction.
options.rationale: Half-remembers the law, keeping 'equal' but losing the opposition of the directions.

options.text: They are equal in size and opposite in direction.
options.rationale: This is the law exactly: whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.

mcqs.stem: A person stands still on a floor. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?

options.text: The floor pushes up on the person; the person pushes down on the floor.
options.rationale: One interaction between two objects, giving forces that are equal, opposite, of the same type, and acting on different objects.

options.text: The floor pushes up on the person; gravity pulls the person down.
options.rationale: The two forces on the free body diagram are equal and opposite, so they look like the pair; both act on the person.

options.text: The person pushes down on the floor; friction acts sideways on them.
options.rationale: Pairs two forces from quite different interactions, chosen when 'two forces, two objects' is applied loosely.

options.text: The person's weight acts downwards; the resultant force on them is zero.
options.rationale: Treats any equal and opposite combination as a pair, without asking which object each force acts on.

mcqs.stem: A car collides head-on with a much heavier lorry. Which statement about the forces during the collision is correct?

options.text: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
options.rationale: Newton's Third Law applies to every interaction; the difference in damage comes from the different masses, not different forces.

options.text: The lorry exerts the larger force because it has far more mass.
options.rationale: Infers the size of the force from the severity of the damage to the car.

options.text: The forces cancel out, so neither vehicle changes its velocity.
options.rationale: Cancels forces that act on different objects, as if they were balanced forces on one body.

options.text: The car exerts the larger force because it is travelling faster.
options.rationale: Substitutes speed for mass as the property that decides which force is bigger.

mcqs.stem: Why can the two forces in a Newton's Third Law pair never cancel each other out?

options.text: They act on two different objects, and not on the same one.
options.rationale: Only forces acting on the same object combine to give a resultant, so a Third Law pair never cancels.

options.text: They act at different times, so they are never present together.
options.rationale: Keeps the idea that a reaction follows an action, so the forces never coincide.

options.text: They are not truly equal in size, only roughly the same size.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who cannot see how exactly equal forces could leave anything free to accelerate.

options.text: One of them is always cancelled by a third force in the system.
options.rationale: Invents an extra force to rescue the cancelling argument rather than questioning it.
